title: Every Polish group has a non-trivial topological group automorphism

predicted_errors.error_location: Title: "Every Polish group has a non-trivial topological group automorphism"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper's own Theorem 1.1 explicitly restricts the result to 'every Polish group with more than two elements.' The trivial group (1 element) and the discrete 2-element group Z₂ are Polish groups whose only automorphism is the identity (Aut(Z₂) = GL₁(Z₂) is trivial, as the paper itself notes when discussing the finite discrete case). Hence the title's unqualified universal claim is false and contradicts the paper's own proven statement.

The abstract states 'We prove that every Polish group admits a non-trivial topological group automorphism' and 'there are no uniquely homogeneous Polish groups,' both without the 'more than two elements' qualifier that appears in Theorem 1.1. Since the 2-element discrete group Z₂ has no non-trivial automorphism, and (as shown below) Z₂ is in fact uniquely homogeneous, both abstract claims are literally false as stated and are contradicted by the paper's own restricted Theorem 1.1.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 3.1 and its surrounding discussion in Section 3: "A non-trivial Polish group cannot be uniquely homogeneous."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 3.1 is stated without the 'more than two elements' restriction required by Theorem 1.1, yet it is derived as a consequence of Theorem 1.1. The 2-element discrete group Z₂ is a non-trivial Polish group, but it is uniquely homogeneous: its only self-homeomorphisms are the identity and the swap map, and for any pair of points there is a unique homeomorphism taking one to the other (the swap for distinct points, the identity for a point to itself). This directly contradicts Theorem 3.1 as stated, exposing a gap between the qualified Theorem 1.1 and the unqualified Theorem 3.1/abstract conclusion.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Lemma 2.3, paragraph constructing V'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof states 'we construct a non-empty open subset V′ ⊆ V for which (x + V′) + (y + V′) = ∅ if x, y ∈ L are distinct' and later '(x + V′) + (y + V′) ⊆ (x+x+Ux) ∩ (y+y+Uy) = ∅.' The operation '+' (sumset) cannot equal the empty set under the stated reasoning; the intended relation is intersection '∩', as used consistently elsewhere in the same proof (e.g., in the definition of 𝒫 and in the verification that W ∈ 𝒫). This mismatched notation makes the stated equalities mathematically meaningless as written and should be corrected to intersection throughout.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3: "Barit and Renaud used the same structural theory of locally compact groups and (non-commutative) Pontryagin duality..."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Pontryagin duality is a classical theory specific to locally compact abelian (LCA) groups; there is no standard theory called '(non-commutative) Pontryagin duality' for general locally compact groups. Attributing such a named duality to the non-abelian setting without further clarification misrepresents standard terminology and may misattribute the actual technique used in the cited work [3].
